title: 論語 學而第一
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 1, 〈學而〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 1 of the Analects, 學而 Xué ér, named, as every book is, from its first words ("To learn, and…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi says this first book records mostly sayings about attending to the root of things — learning, family duty, good faith — as the gateway to the rest. Each numbered passage (1.1–1.16, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
學而時習之，
不亦說乎？

morph.gloss: the Master — on its own as a speaker, always Confucius
in season, at the right times

sentences.l:
The Master said: “To learn, and in season rehearse it —
is it not indeed a delight?
sentences.i: The Master said: “Learning, and going over it again each time its season comes round — is that not a delight?
sentences.n: The first words of the book. 子 'the Master', standing alone as speaker, is always Confucius. Three things you will meet on every page: 而 joins two verbs ('learn AND THEN rehearse'); 之 after a verb is an object pronoun, 'it'; and 不亦…乎 'is it not indeed…?' is a rhetorical question expecting yes — the whole passage is three of them. 說 here is the word 'delighted', read yuè and later written 悅; the reading shuō 'to speak' would make nonsense. Zhu Xi takes 習 from its picture, a fledgling beating its wings 羽 over and over: learning is rehearsed until it becomes your own. 時 is 'at the proper times' or 'constantly' — the commentators give both.

sentences.t:
有朋自遠方來，
不亦樂乎？
sentences.l:
To have companions from distant parts come —
is it not indeed a joy?
sentences.i: When companions come from distant parts, is that not a cause for gladness?
sentences.n: Same shape as the line before: a clause stated as a topic, then 不亦…乎. 朋 is narrower than 'friend': Bao Xian's old gloss, preserved in He Yan's commentary, is 同門曰朋 'those who share one gate (one master) are called 朋', and Zhu Xi has 同類 'one's own kind'. 樂 is read lè 'joy' here; the same character is yuè 'music', which you will meet often.

sentences.t:
人不知而不慍，
不亦君子乎？」

morph.gloss: a gentleman — a man of cultivated character
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Others do not know (him), and yet (he) does not resent —
is it not indeed a gentleman?”
sentences.i: To go unrecognized by others and bear no grudge for it — is that not what a gentleman is?”
sentences.n: Classical Chinese leaves out any subject or object the context supplies: 人不知 is just 'others not know', and the 'him' (or 'you') is ours. 而 here is 'and yet' — the same joining word as in the first line, now joining two things you would not expect together. 君子 is the book's central figure. Literally 'a lord's son', a man of birth; in the Analects it is a man of cultivated character, whatever his birth. 'Gentleman' carries the same double history in English, which is why we keep it.

sentences.t:
有子曰：「
其為人也孝弟，
而好犯上者，鮮矣；
不好犯上，
而好作亂者，未之有也。

morph.gloss: Master You — the disciple You Ruo
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
deferential to elders — a younger brother's duty (later written 悌 tì)
it (object pronoun, moved before the verb)

sentences.l:
Master You said: “As for being a man, filial and deferential,
and yet fond of defying superiors — few indeed;
not fond of defying superiors,
and yet fond of raising disorder — never yet has it been.
sentences.i: Master You said: “Of those who are good sons and dutiful younger brothers, few are inclined to defy their superiors; and among those not inclined to defy their superiors, there has never been one inclined to stir up rebellion.
sentences.n: 有子 is You Ruo 有若, one of only two disciples the book calls 'Master' (the other is Zeng Shen, in 1.4); the title suggests their own followers had a hand in recording these sayings. 孝 and 弟 are a pair you will meet again and again: 孝 xiào is devotion to one's parents, 弟 (read tì, later written 悌) the deference a younger brother owes his elders. 者 turns what goes before into a noun: 好犯上者 'the ones fond of defying superiors'. 未之有也 shows a rule worth learning now — in a negative sentence a pronoun object jumps in front of the verb: not 未有之 but 未之有, 'not-yet it have'.

sentences.t:
君子務本，
本立而道生。
孝弟也者，
其為仁之本與？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
(with 也: 'as for…' — the pair sets up what goes before as the topic)

sentences.l:
The gentleman works at the root;
the root established, and the Way grows.
Filiality and deference —
are they not the root of practising humaneness?”
sentences.i: The gentleman devotes himself to the root, for once the root stands firm, the Way grows from it. Being a good son and a good younger brother — is that not the root of humaneness?”
sentences.n: 仁 rén, humaneness, is the virtue the whole Analects turns on: the quality that makes one fully human toward others. It is defined nowhere and illustrated everywhere; 'humaneness' is our standing rendering. 為仁 is Zhu Xi's reading, 'practising humaneness' (為仁猶曰行仁), which spares Master You from saying that family duty is the source of humaneness itself. 也者 together mark a topic ('as for…'), and the closing 與 (read yú, later written 歟) makes the statement a modest question — Zhu Xi: 'a word of doubt, too humble to assert'. Variant: one of our collation witnesses reads 為人之本 'the root of being a person', and He Yan's text drops 為.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
巧言令色，
鮮矣仁！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Clever words, a pleasing face —
rare indeed, humaneness!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Smooth talk and a face put on to please: seldom is there humaneness in them.”
sentences.n: Look at the order. Plain prose would put the subject first (仁鮮矣 'humaneness is rare'); here the predicate 鮮矣 jumps ahead and 仁 is left to land last, which gives the saying its sting. 色 is the colour of the face — the expression a man puts on. Zhu Xi adds that 'rare' is the sage's mild way of saying 'none at all'. The same saying returns word for word at 17.17.

sentences.t:
曾子曰：「
吾日三省吾身：
為人謀而不忠乎？
與朋友交而不信乎？
傳不習乎？」

morph.gloss: Master Zeng — the disciple Zeng Shen
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
what was handed on — the teaching received

sentences.l:
Master Zeng said: “I daily on three points examine my person:
for others planning, and not wholehearted?
with friends dealing, and not true to my word?
what was handed on, not rehearsed?”
sentences.i: Master Zeng said: “Each day I search my conduct on three matters. In making plans for others, have I held anything back? In my dealings with friends, have I failed to keep my word? What my teacher handed on to me — have I failed to practise it?”
sentences.n: 曾子 is Zeng Shen 曾參, among the youngest disciples, the second to be called 'Master'. 三省 can be 'examine three times' or 'on three points'; Zhu Xi takes it as the three matters that follow, and so do we. Two words that pair often: 忠 zhōng, giving all of oneself (Zhu Xi: 盡己 'exhausting oneself'), and 信 xìn, being true to one's word. 為 here is wèi 'for, on behalf of'. 傳不習乎 is read by Zhu Xi as 'what was handed on to me by my teacher, have I not rehearsed it?' — the 習 of 1.1 again. Another old reading takes it as 'have I handed on what I have not practised myself?' He Yan's text reads 交言而不信 here, 'in dealing with friends, my WORDS not true'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
道千乘之國：
敬事而信，
節用而愛人，
使民以時。」

morph.gloss: to lead, to govern (= 導 dǎo)
others — here, those who serve under him

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Leading a state of a thousand chariots:
reverent in affairs and keeping faith,
measured in spending and cherishing others,
employing the people according to the seasons.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “To govern a state of a thousand chariots: attend to its business with reverent care and keep faith; be sparing in expenditure and cherish those who serve; and call on the common folk for labour only in the proper season.”
sentences.n: 道 is here a verb, 'to lead, to govern' — the word later written 導 dǎo, and read so in modern practice. A state's size was reckoned by the war chariots it could field; 千乘之國 is a major feudal state. Notice 人 and 民 side by side: 人 'others, people' and 民 'the common folk' are not the same, and many readers take 人 here as the ruler's officers and 民 as the farming population. 使民以時: Zhu Xi explains it as calling men to corvée labour only in the slack farming season.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
弟子入則孝，
出則弟，
謹而信，
汎愛衆，
而親仁。
行有餘力，
則以學文。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “At home the young should serve their parents well, and out in the world defer to their elders; be careful in conduct and true to their word; have love for everyone, and keep close to those who are humane. If, after all this, they have strength left over, let them spend it on study of the literary arts.”
sentences.n: The two 弟 are read differently, and Zhu Xi says so: in 弟子 'the young' it is dì 'younger brother', in 出則弟 it is tì, the duty a younger brother owes. 則 'then' links condition and consequence: 入則孝 'going in, then filial'. 仁 at the end is the humane themselves, the quality standing for the people who have it. 文 is the whole literary inheritance — Zhu Xi lists the Odes, the Documents and the six arts. The order is the point: conduct first, books with what is left over.

sentences.t:
子夏曰：「
賢賢易色；
事父母，能竭其力；
事君，能致其身；
與朋友交，言而有信。
雖曰未學，
吾必謂之學矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
in exchange for, in place of

sentences.i: Zixia said: “A man who esteems worth in place of beauty, who spends all his strength in serving his parents, who gives his very person in serving his lord, and whose word holds good in his dealings with friends — though others may say he has had no schooling, I would certainly say he is learned.”
sentences.n: 子夏 Zixia is Bu Shang 卜商, the disciple best known for learning in the texts — which makes his claim pointed: learning is shown in conduct. 賢賢易色 is famous for its difficulty. The first 賢 is a verb, 'to treat as worthy', the second its object, 'the worthy' — the part-of-speech fluidity you met in 1.5's 道. Zhu Xi takes 易色 as 'in exchange for the love of beauty': a man who loves worth the way others love a beautiful face. Others read 易 as 'to change' (he alters his expression in a worthy man's presence) or take the line as about a husband's regard for his wife. We follow Zhu Xi.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子不重則不威，
學則不固。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “A gentleman not weighty, then not commanding respect;
his learning, then, not firm.
sentences.i: The Master said: “A gentleman without gravity commands no respect, and what he learns does not hold fast.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi reads both clauses as one thought: a man light in his outward bearing cannot be firm within, so his learning does not set either. An older reading, Kong Anguo's in He Yan's commentary, takes 固 as 'blinkered' and splits the line: 'if he learns, he will not be narrow'. We follow Zhu Xi, whose text this is, and note the other.

sentences.t: 主忠信。

morph.gloss: to hold as chief, take as first principle

sentences.l: Take as chief wholeheartedness and good faith.
sentences.i: Hold to wholeheartedness and good faith above all.
sentences.n: Three characters, a whole maxim: no subject, no connective. 主 is 'host, master', used as a verb — 'make it the master', 'put it first'. 忠 and 信 are the pair from 1.4.

sentences.t: 無友不如己者。

morph.gloss: to come up to, be equal to

sentences.l: Do not befriend those not equal to oneself.
sentences.i: Do not make friends of those who fall short of you.
sentences.n: 無 is here a prohibition, the word usually written 毋 'do not!' — Zhu Xi says so (無毋通). 友 'friend' is the verb 'to befriend'. Zhu Xi's reason: a friend is there to help you toward humaneness, and one who falls short of you cannot. Readers have long been uneasy that, taken strictly, no friendship could then be mutual; some read 如 as 'to be like (in aims)' — befriend no one unlike yourself.

sentences.t: 過則勿憚改。」
sentences.l: Erring, then do not shrink from correcting.”
sentences.i: When you go astray, do not shrink from setting it right.”
sentences.n: 勿 is the plain prohibitive 'do not'. 過 is first 'to go past' and so 'to overstep, to err'. The same line returns in Book 9 (子罕).

sentences.t:
曾子曰：「
慎終追遠，
民德歸厚矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the end — a parent's death and its rites
to follow after — to honour with offerings

sentences.l:
Master Zeng said: “Careful with the end, following after the distant —
the people's virtue returns to fullness.”
sentences.i: Master Zeng said: “Attend with care to the rites when a parent dies, and keep up the offerings to ancestors long gone, and the people's virtue will grow deep again.”
sentences.n: Four characters carry the whole first half, and the commentary supplies what they mean: 終 'the end' is a parent's death and the mourning rites, 遠 'the distant' the ancestors honoured with sacrifice. Zhu Xi's point is that both are easily neglected, which is why care for them shows depth. 德 dé is virtue, the moral quality that shows in conduct; the people's virtue 'returns' to depth because it was once there.

sentences.t:
子禽問於子貢曰：「
夫子至於是邦也，
必聞其政，
求之與？
抑與之與？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Ziqin asked of Zigong, saying: “The Master, arriving at this state or that,
is sure to hear of its government.
Does he seek it?
Or do they give it to him?”
sentences.i: Ziqin asked Zigong: “Whatever state our Master comes to, he always comes to learn how it is governed. Does he ask for this, or is it offered to him?”
sentences.n: 子禽 is Chen Kang 陳亢; Zhu Xi notes that some made him Zigong's disciple rather than Confucius's, and says no one can tell. 子貢 Zigong, Duanmu Ci 端木賜, eloquent and rich from trade, is one of the most quoted disciples. 夫子 'the Master' — literally 'that master' — is how the disciples refer to Confucius. Watch the two 與 in 抑與之與: the first is the verb yǔ 'to give', the second the question particle yú (later written 歟). Same graph, two words.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
夫子溫﹑良﹑恭﹑儉﹑讓以得之。
夫子之求之也，
其諸異乎人之求之與？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
(makes 'the Master seeks it' into a noun phrase)

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “The Master — gentle, good, courteous, restrained, deferential — thereby gets it.
The Master's seeking of it —
surely it differs from others' seeking of it?”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “Our Master gets it by being gentle, straightforward, courteous, restrained and deferential. If this is seeking, surely it is unlike the way other men seek.”
sentences.n: Five one-character virtues in a row, then 以 'thereby'. Zhu Xi glosses each: 溫 mild and generous, 良 easy and direct, 恭 grave and reverent, 儉 self-restrained, 讓 modest. 之 does a new job here: placed between a subject and its verb (夫子之求之 'the Master's seeking it'), it turns a whole sentence into a noun phrase that can then be talked about. 乎 after a verb of comparison is a preposition, 'from, than', the same as 於. 其諸 is a softening particle, 'surely, perhaps'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
父在，觀其志；
父沒，觀其行；
三年無改於父之道，
可謂孝矣。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “While a man's father lives, look at what he aims at; when his father is gone, look at what he does. If for three years he makes no change to his father's ways, he may be called a good son.”
sentences.n: Whose intent and whose conduct? Zhu Xi: the son's. While the father lives the son cannot act on his own, so only his aims can be seen; afterwards his deeds show. 三年 is the mourning period for a parent (counted, in practice, as into the third year). 可謂 'can be called' — 可 before a verb makes it passive in sense: 'can be called', not 'can call'. Zhu Xi reads 行 here as xìng, the old tone for 'conduct'; modern reading practice does not keep that distinction, so we give xíng, as the Daodejing gives 難 nán.

sentences.t:
有子曰：「
禮之用，和為貴。
先王之道，斯為美；
小大由之。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Master You said: “In the practice of the rites, ease is what matters most. This was what made the way of the former kings fine, and in matters small and great they went by it.
sentences.n: 禮 lǐ, the rites, is the third great term of the book: ceremony and ritual, and with them the whole body of right custom and manners. 和 is usually rendered 'harmony'; Zhu Xi explains it as 從容不迫 'easy and unhurried', the relaxed bearing that keeps strict forms from becoming stiff, and we follow him. 先王 'the former kings' are the sage rulers of antiquity. 為 is wéi 'to count as, to be' in both lines.

sentences.t:
有所不行：
知和而和，
不以禮節之，
亦不可行也。」
sentences.l:
There are cases where it will not do:
knowing ease and being at ease,
not using the rites to keep it in bounds —
that too cannot work.”
sentences.i: Yet there are times when it will not do: to seek ease for ease's sake, without holding it within the bounds of the rites — that will not do either.”
sentences.n: 所 turns the verb phrase after it into a noun: 有所不行 'there is that-which does-not-work'. 知和而和 is a verb repeated as noun and verb: 'knowing ease and so (simply) being at ease'. 節 is first a joint in bamboo, and so 'a measure, to keep within measure'. The two halves of the passage balance each other: the rites need ease, and ease needs the rites.

sentences.t:
有子曰：「
信近於義，言可復也；
恭近於禮，遠恥辱也；
因不失其親，
亦可宗也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
relying on, those one depends on
those one should be close to
be looked up to as head

sentences.l:
Master You said: “Good faith close to what is right — words can be made good.
Courtesy close to the rites — keeps shame and disgrace far.
Relying, not missing those one should be close to —
they too can be taken as one's head.”
sentences.i: Master You said: “When the promises you make stay close to what is right, your word can be kept. When your courtesy stays close to the rites, shame and disgrace are kept far off. When those you depend on are people fit to be close to, you can look up to them as your head.”
sentences.n: 義 yì is what is right — Zhu Xi: 事之宜 'what fits the affair'. 復 is 'to go back over' and so 'to make good (one's word)'. The third line is the hardest in the book so far; we follow Zhu Xi, who reads 因 as 'to depend on' (依) and 宗 as 'to take as one's chief' (主). Zhu Xi reads 遠 here in the falling tone, yuàn, the old reading of the verb 'to keep far off'; we give yuǎn, as modern practice does.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子食無求飽，
居無求安，
敏於事而慎於言，
就有道而正焉，
可謂好學也已。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: The Master said: “A gentleman who does not look to eat his fill or to live in comfort, who is prompt in action and careful in speech, and who goes to those who have the Way to be set right by them — such a man may truly be called fond of learning.”
sentences.n: 無 here is plain 'not', not the prohibition of 1.8 — context decides. 焉 is a fused word, 於之 'at it, by them': 正焉 'is corrected by them'. The closing 也 + 已 piles a particle of finality on one of assertion; it adds no word to the English, only a full stop said with conviction. Once again 'learning' is shown in how a man eats, lives and speaks. He Yan's text reads 也巳矣 here.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
貧而無諂，
富而無驕，
何如？」子曰：「
可也；
未若貧而樂，
富而好禮者也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
how is it? what would you say?
to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “Poor yet without fawning,
rich yet without arrogance —
how is it?” The Master said: “Acceptable;
not yet as good as poor yet joyful,
rich yet fond of the rites.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “To be poor without fawning and rich without arrogance — what would you say of that?” The Master said: “It will do. But it is not as good as being poor and joyful, rich and fond of the rites.”
sentences.n: Zigong grew rich in trade (Zhu Xi notes that he was poor first, and speaks from experience). 何如 is a fixed question, 'how is it?', asking for a judgement. 可也 is faint praise, 'passable'. 未若 'not yet like' is the standard way to say 'not as good as'. Variant: both of our collation witnesses, and many later editions, read 貧而樂道 'poor yet delighting in the Way'. Zhu Xi's text has no 道, and we print his text.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「《詩》云：『
如切如磋，
如琢如磨。』
其斯之謂與？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
surely, is it — (opens a tentative question)

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “The Odes say:
‘As cut, as filed;
as carved, as polished.’
Is it this that is meant?”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “The Odes say: ‘Like bone cut and then filed, like jade carved and then polished.’ Is that what you mean?”
sentences.n: 詩 is the Odes, the Book of Songs, a collection of 305 ancient poems; the couplet is from 淇奧 'The Bends of the Qi' (Odes 55). Zhu Xi explains the craft: horn and bone are cut and then filed, jade and stone carved and then polished — good work made finer still. That is Zigong's point: 'not fawning' is good; 'joyful' is the same thing polished. 其斯之謂與 is another fronted object: 斯 'this' is what is 'meant' (謂), moved forward and marked by 之 — 'is it THIS that is meant?'

sentences.t:
子曰：「
賜也，
始可與言《詩》已矣！
告諸往而知來者。」

morph.gloss: (pause after a name: 'as for you, Ci')
at last, now for the first time

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Ci —
at last I can talk about the Odes with you!
Tell (you) what has gone, and (you) know what is to come.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Ci, now at last I can talk about the Odes with you. Tell you what has gone before, and you see what is to come.”
sentences.n: 賜 Ci is Zigong's personal name: a teacher may use it; others use the courtesy name 子貢. 已 + 矣 doubles the sense of finality, a teacher's satisfaction made audible. 諸 is another fused word, 之於 'it to': 告諸往 'tell it — the past — to (him)'. Zhu Xi: 'what has gone' is what was said, 'what is to come' what was not said.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不患人之不己知，
患不知人也。」

morph.gloss: (makes 'others do not know me' into a noun phrase)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Be not troubled by others' not knowing oneself;
be troubled by not knowing others.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Be troubled not that others do not know you, but that you do not know them.”
sentences.n: Book 1 ends where it began, with 人不知 'others do not know' from 1.1. Two rules you have met come together: 之 between subject and verb makes 人之不己知 one noun phrase, 'others' not-knowing-one', and in a negative sentence the pronoun object 己 moves before the verb (不己知, not 不知己), as 之 did in 1.2's 未之有也.
